title: Writing RFCs
description: Learn how to write effective Request for Comments documents to propose, refine, and gain alignment on technical changes before implementation.

data.text: An RFC, or Request for Comments, is a document that proposes a technical change and invites feedback before any code is written. It is one of the most powerful tools a senior engineer has for making better decisions and avoiding costly mistakes. A well-written RFC aligns the team, surfaces edge cases early, and creates a durable record of why a decision was made.

The RFC process works because it separates proposal from implementation. Instead of debating details in pull requests after weeks of coding, the team debates ideas when the cost of change is low. This leads to faster development, fewer surprises, and better solutions.

Not every change needs an RFC. Use the rule of thumb: if the change is reversible and affects only your team, a design doc or informal discussion is enough. Write an RFC when the change is hard to reverse, affects multiple teams, involves significant cost or risk, or touches core architecture.

data.title: RFC vs Design Doc vs ADR
data.content: Choosing the right format for technical proposals.
data.code:
RFC (Request for Comments):
- Scope: Large, cross-team, or irreversible changes
- Audience: Multiple teams, engineering leadership
- Process: Written proposal, async feedback, formal approval
- Example: Migrating from monolith to microservices

Design Doc:
- Scope: Medium changes within one team
- Audience: Immediate team and closely affected teams
- Process: Lightweight doc, quick feedback loop
- Example: Adding a new API endpoint to an existing service

ADR (Architecture Decision Record):
- Scope: Documenting a decision already made
- Audience: Future maintainers of the system
- Process: Brief record of context, decision, and consequences
- Example: Choosing PostgreSQL over MySQL for a new service

data.text: The Structure of a Good RFC

A good RFC tells a story. It explains the problem, presents a clear solution, discusses alternatives honestly, and describes how success will be measured. Most RFCs follow a simple structure: summary, motivation, proposal, alternatives, drawbacks, rollout plan, and success metrics.

data.title: RFC Template
data.content: A practical template for writing effective RFCs.
data.code:
# RFC 123: Adopt Event Sourcing for Order Management

## Summary
Replace the current order-state model with event sourcing to improve auditability and enable new analytics features.

## Motivation
- Current system makes it difficult to answer "what changed and when?"
- Product team requests historical order analysis features
- Event sourcing is a proven pattern at our scale

## Proposal
1. Introduce an events table capturing all order mutations
2. Migrate existing orders via a one-time backfill
3. Update order service to read from events, not direct state
4. Add event replay capability for debugging

## Detailed Design
- Event schema and versioning strategy
- Migration steps and rollback plan
- New infrastructure requirements

## Alternatives Considered
1. Add audit triggers to existing tables — simpler but less flexible
2. Use CDC from database — proven but adds operational complexity
3. Append-only log in application — good, but event sourcing is more standard

## Drawbacks
- Increased storage costs (estimated 3x current)
- Steeper learning curve for new team members
- More complex deployment (two-phase migration)

## Rollout Plan
1. Week 1-2: Event schema review and team alignment
2. Week 3-4: Prototype in staging environment
3. Week 5-6: Canary deploy to production
4. Week 7: Full rollout with feature flag

## Success Metrics
- Zero data loss during migration
- Query latency for order history under 200ms
- Ability to replay 30 days of events in under 5 minutes

data.text: Your reader is busy. Write for clarity, not completeness. Use short paragraphs, bullet points, and concrete examples. Avoid jargon unless your audience uses it daily. If a section feels long, split it into subsections. The RFC should be skimmable because reviewers will skim it first.

data.title: The 10-Minute Test
data.text: If a senior engineer cannot understand the core proposal in 10 minutes, your RFC is too long or too vague. Start with a one-paragraph summary that answers: what, why, and what happens if we do nothing.

Feedback on an RFC is a gift, even when it feels critical. Respond to every comment, even if only to say "acknowledged." When you disagree, explain why. When you change the proposal, update the RFC so the document reflects the current state. The RFC becomes the source of truth for the decision.

items: Address concerns directly rather than defensively
Update the RFC when the proposal changes
Close the loop on every thread before approving

data.text: RFCs work only if the culture supports them. The document must be a safe space for honest feedback, not a stage for defending ideas. Leaders set the tone by writing clear RFCs themselves, responding graciously to criticism, and rewarding people who raise valid concerns early. The goal is better decisions, not winning arguments.

terms.definition: A written proposal for a technical change that is reviewed and discussed before implementation begins.
A short document that records a single architectural decision, its context, and its consequences.
A mechanism to enable or disable a feature at runtime without deploying code, used to reduce risk during rollouts.

data.title: Avoid RFC Theatre
data.text: An RFC that rubber-stamps a decision already made wastes everyone time. Write the RFC before the decision is fixed, leave room for the proposal to change, and genuinely consider feedback. If you already know the answer, skip the RFC.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Use RFCs for large, irreversible, or cross-team changes
Write a one-paragraph summary first — what, why, and what if we do nothing
Discuss alternatives honestly, including the simplest option
Include a clear rollout plan and measurable success criteria
Respond to every comment and update the RFC as it evolves
Build a culture where raising concerns early is rewarded
data.takeaway: RFCs convert tribal knowledge into documented decisions, reduce implementation risk, and build team alignment before any code is written.
